subject: Correction of p-value for defined parameters in multi-group analysis

messages.author: b07c7c226b1dfae8
messages.subject: Correction of p-value for defined parameters in multi-group analysis
parts:
Dear All,

I have two groups of samples and one model. My aim is to identify path coefficients in the model that are significantly different between these two groups.

Here is an example:

> mod
      [,1]                          
 [1,] "X1 ~ c(a1_1, a1_2)*X2"   
 [2,] "d1 := a1_1 - a1_2"           
 [3,] "X1 ~ c(a2_1, a2_2)*X3"   
 [4,] "d2 := a2_1 - a2_2"           
 [5,] "X2 ~ c(a3_1, a3_2)*X3"  
 [6,] "d3 := a3_1 - a3_2"           
           
fit <-  sem(mod, data = my_data, meanstructure = TRUE , fixed.x = FALSE, group = 'group')

summary(fit)

Defined Parameters:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
    d1                0.152    0.209    0.728    0.467
    d2               -0.626    0.154   -4.055    0.020
    d3               -0.037    0.188   -0.195    0.845


With the 0.05 threshold I may say that two groups are significantly different in the "X1 <- X3" path coefficient. 
On the other hand, I've tested three path coefficients, hence, what do you think, should I correct obtained p-values for multiple testing?

Anna.

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Correction of p-value for defined parameters in multi-group analysis
parts: On the other hand, I've tested three path coefficients, hence, what do you think, should I correct obtained p-values for multiple testing?

Depends what you define as a "family" of tests.  If you consider the 3 slopes to be different "families" of hypotheses, then the familywise error rate doesn't need correction because it is only one test per family.  If these equality constraints are in the same family (e.g., distinct from the family of tests of whether the estimates are zero), then divide alpha by the number of tests in that family (3). If you want to control the experimentwise error rate, then you need to divide alpha by however many tests you plan to conduct altogether.  There's no right answer; it's just a matter of which particular error rate you want to control (i.e., out of which specific set of tests do you only want a 5% chance of at least one Type I error, or a 95% chance of no Type I errors in the set?).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: Correction of p-value for defined parameters in multi-group analysis
parts:
I am curious whether or why the Bonferoni procedure would be preferable to protected tests.  I was under the impression that the Bonferoni procedure was not the preferable procedure due to low power.  I would have instead first constrained all the parameters of interest to equality across groups as an omnibus test.  If the constrained model fit as well as the unconstrained model, I would have concluded that equality across groups was plausible for all the parameters and not run individual tests.  If the constrained model fit less well, then I would have run the individual tests on each parameter and used their p values as reported.

So, I am curious, am I mistaken to believe that the protected test procedure is preferable to the Bonferoni adjustment?  Is there a problem with the protected test procedure in this context?

Keith

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Correction of p-value for defined parameters in multi-group analysis
parts: So, I am curious, am I mistaken to believe that the protected test procedure is preferable to the Bonferoni adjustment?  Is there a problem with the protected test procedure in this context?

I agree.  I think the best route would be to use labels to constrain all parameters to equality and assess whether model fit is equivalent using anova().

http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/groups.html

If that test is significant, indicating at least one of the parameters differs, a Bonferroni adjustment could be used for individual follow-up tests, either by fitting models with a single constraint added, or by using lavTestScore() on the constrained model to see which constraints have a significant modification index.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
